newsitem.title: KENYA: Rwanda gets 280 new judges as genocide cases pile up.
newsitem.headline: Rwanda gets 280 new judges as genocide cases pile up.

text.p: About 280 new judges and magistrates were sworn in on Saturday in Rwanda, to revive a judicial system that collapsed when millions fled the country in 1994 after a wave of genocide, Rwandan radio reported.
The judges, who were sworn in before the prime minister, include 20 supreme court judges and a larger number who will serve in lower courts, the radio said in a broadcast monitored in Nairobi.

"Government officials who attended the ceremony expressed their confidence that problems in the judicial sector, especially the lack of manpower, will now be solved. They appealed to the judges who were sworn in to work for justice and to be exemplary in fostering true justice in the country," the radio said.

Virtually all the former judges and magistrates fled Rwanda in 1994 after the genocide in which up to a million minority Tutsis and moderate Hutus were killed. The police force and the court system collapsed.

The Hutu-dominated government that instigated the genocide was defeated in civil war and replaced by a new government set up by the mainly Tutsi Rwanda Patriotic Front (RPF), whose forces had invaded from neighbouring Uganda in 1990.

An estimated 80,000 Rwandan Hutus have been arrested since the RPF takeover, on charges of organising or participating in the 1994 genocide attacks. They are held in overcrowded jails throughout the country, in conditions widely condemned by humanitarian groups.
The government has adopted a Genocide Law, the crucial text for deciding levels of guilt and punishment in trials for years to come.
"We are making the last arrangements to start trials," Gerard Gahima, the acting minister of justice, told Reuters in Kigali recently.

Pursuing its own process, the U.N.-appointed International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda, with its court based in Tanzania, also intends to try those accused of genocide. But so far it has only indicted 21 suspects, of whom 11 are in custody.
